questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Inverse of an Orthogonal Matrix
questions.problem: Find the inverse of the orthogonal matrix $D=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5} \\ -\frac{4}{5} & \frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
The inverse of an orthogonal matrix is equal to its transpose.

Therefore, since $D$ is orthogonal, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}^{-1} & ={D}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5} & -\frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5} & \frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements About Orthogonal Matrices
questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the $n\times n$ orthogonal matrices $P$ and $Q?$

- $2PQ$ is always orthogonal
- $P-Q$ is always orthogonal
- $P$ is **not** invertible
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $Q$ is orthogonal if and only if

$$
Q{Q}^{T}={Q}^{T}Q=I.
$$

To check that a matrix is orthogonal, it is sufficient to check that the above equation is satisfied.

Moreover, we have the following properties:

- For any orthogonal matrix $Q,$ we have ${Q}^{-1}={Q}^{T}.$

- $(AB)^{T}={B}^{T}{A}^{T}$ for conformable matrices $A$ and $B.$

With that in mind, let's inspect each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Computing the product $(2PQ)\cdot (2PQ)^{T},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(2PQ)\cdot (2PQ)^{T} & =2PQ\cdot 2{Q}^{T}{P}^{T} \\  & =4P(Q{Q}^{T}){P}^{T} \\  & =4P(I){P}^{T} \\  & =4I \\  & \ne I.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. As a counterexample, consider the following subtraction of two orthogonal matrices:

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

The resulting matrix is not orthogonal since, for example, its first column is not normalized.

- Statement III is false. The inverse of an orthogonal matrix $P$ is given by ${P}^{-1}={P}^{T}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true".

choices.value: None of the statements are true

answer_fields.correct_value: None of the statements are true

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements About Orthogonal Matrices
questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the $n\times n$ orthogonal matrices $P$ and $Q?$

- $Q$ is invertible
- ${P}^{T}$ is orthogonal
- ${Q}^{-1}$ is always orthogonal
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $Q$ is orthogonal if and only if

$$
Q{Q}^{T}={Q}^{T}Q=I.
$$

To check that a matrix is orthogonal, it is sufficient to check that the above equation is satisfied.

Moreover, we have the following properties:

- For any orthogonal matrix $Q,$ we have ${Q}^{-1}={Q}^{T}.$

- $(AB)^{T}={B}^{T}{A}^{T}$ for conformable matrices $A$ and $B.$

With that in mind, let's inspect each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. The inverse of an orthogonal matrix $Q$ is given by ${Q}^{-1}={Q}^{T}.$

- Statement II is true. Computing the product ${P}^{T}\cdot ({P}^{T})^{T},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{T}\cdot ({P}^{T})^{T} & ={P}^{T}\cdot P \\  & =I.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Computing the product ${Q}^{-1}\cdot ({Q}^{-1})^{T},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}^{-1}\cdot ({Q}^{-1})^{T} & ={Q}^{T}\cdot ({Q}^{T})^{T} \\  & ={Q}^{T}Q \\  & =I.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Determinant of a Product of Matrices
questions.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{5}{\sqrt{61}} & \frac{6}{\sqrt{61}} \\ \frac{6}{\sqrt{61}} & \frac{5}{\sqrt{61}}\end{aligned}],\,Q=[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{13} & 2 \\ 0 & \sqrt{5}\end{aligned}]
$$

Find $|\text{det}(PQ)|$ given that $P$ is an orthogonal matrix.
questions.worked_solution:
We use the following facts: 

- The determinant of a product is equal to the product of the determinants.

- The determinant of an orthogonal matrix $P$ is equal to $\pm 1.$

Applying these ideas, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\text{det}(PQ)| & =|\text{det}(P)\cdot \text{det}(Q)| \\  & =|(\pm 1)\cdot \text{det}(Q)| \\  & =|\pm 1|\cdot |\text{det}(Q)| \\  & =|\text{det}(Q)| \\  & =|\sqrt{13}\cdot \sqrt{5}-0\cdot 2| \\  & =\sqrt{65}\end{aligned}
$$
